settings.prompt:
Autonomously review this Java source repository for potential security
vulnerabilities using the available read-only tools. Do not ask the user questions or summarize
tool output. Copy exact relative paths from list_files or index results; never invent or prefix a path.
A file listing or index hint is only navigation; inspect original source and seek
counter-evidence before deciding. Trace plausible untrusted input to security-sensitive
operations where possible, and check relevant guards and configuration. Report at most 10
candidates supported by exact source lines, with root cause, preconditions, counter-evidence,
and missing evidence. Do not assume a vulnerability exists. If source review finds no supported
candidate, submit an empty candidate list. Your final action must be submit_findings; natural
language commentary is not a report. Do not use project names, dataset identifiers, or a guessed
known answer as evidence.

counter_evidence: Default import count is 1 (Policy.java:70, ExternalCssScanner.java:101-104), which limits volume but not destination.
Response size is capped by getResponseBody(sizeLimit) and HttpContentTooLargeException is handled (ExternalCssScanner.java:129-143).
Connection and socket timeouts are configured from the policy connectionTimeout directive with DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=1000ms (CssScanner.java:58, ExternalCssScanner.java:89-99), reducing blocking risk.
The feature is gated behind the policy directive embedStyleSheets; AntiSamyDOMScanner uses plain CssScanner when it is false (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:397-400).
Inline style attributes are always scanned with the non-importing CssScanner (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:538-542), so this path is limited to <style> blocks.
candidates.description: ExternalCssScanner.parseImportedStylesheets pulls every URI that the CSS @import-rule handling queued into the `stylesheets` LinkedList and issues an HTTP GET for it (ExternalCssScanner.java:108-131). The only controls applied are (a) an import-count cap (allowedImports, default Policy.DEFAULT_MAX_STYLESHEET_IMPORTS=1, lines 101-122) and (b) a total response-size cap via stylesheetRequest.getResponseBody(sizeLimit) (lines 129-158). There is no scheme, host/IP or private-range allow-list, and the fetched bytes are then handed back into the CSS parser (parser.parseStyleSheet, lines 160-168). Because the URI text originates from attacker-controllable stylesheet content, if the deployment reaches this method the caller can cause the server to make outbound requests to arbitrary URIs. The method only runs when the policy enables external stylesheets: AntiSamyDOMScanner.processStyleTag selects ExternalCssScanner when policy.isEmbedStyleSheets() is true, otherwise it uses the non-importing CssScanner (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:397-400, invoked from actionValidate at lines 359-361). CssScanner.scanStyleSheet in turn always calls parseImportedStylesheets after parsing (CssScanner.java:150), so the import queue is consumed whenever the policy permits imports. Full documentation that this is the known SSRF-adjacent issue: only source was read, no advisory text.
missing_evidence: The read spans excluded CssHandler.java, which is what actually populates the stylesheets LinkedList; I did not verify whether it filters/validates the URI before queuing it.
I did not read Policy/InternalPolicy getters to confirm whether any additional import allow-list directive exists that could constrain destination URIs.
No deployment/default policy XML was inspected to establish whether embedStyleSheets is commonly enabled.
Reachability of @import parsing in this repo version was not proven by running code.
preconditions: Any scanned HTML contains a <style> element that survives into processStyleTag (tag rule action 'validate', AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:359-361).
The active policy sets the embedStyleSheets directive to true so ExternalCssScanner is instantiated (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:397-399).
The policy's maxStyleSheetImports directive is >= 1 (or unset, giving DEFAULT_MAX_STYLESHEET_IMPORTS = 1) so the size-limit/count guards do not block the fetch (ExternalCssScanner.java:101-122).
Attacker can control CSS content containing an @import of an arbitrary URI (or influence the parser to queue one).
candidates.title: ExternalCssScanner fetches @import stylesheet URIs without scheme/host allow-listing (SSRF / local file access)

counter_evidence: DocumentBuilderFactory in both getPolicy and getTopLevelElement disables external general/parameter entities, disallows DOCTYPE and disables external DTD loading (Policy.java:287-290, 372-375), so the include open is not driven by XML entity expansion.
Includes are only honored by URL/File-based factories; the InputStream and String-filename overloads route through getSimpleParseContext, which throws if includes are present (Policy.java:226-231).
MalformedURLException and FileNotFoundException are caught and treated as no-ops (Policy.java:343-364), so failure does not surface as an exception-based oracle in this snippet.
candidates.description: Policy.getParseContext iterates <include> elements and passes the href attribute to getPolicy (Policy.java:246-251). getPolicy constructs `new URL(baseUrl, href)` (or falls back to URIUtils.resolveAsString) and unconditionally opens the stream with url.openStream() before parsing it with a securely configured DocumentBuilderFactory (Policy.java:335-364 and 367-383). There is no scheme restriction (file:, http:, jar:, ftp: are all accepted by the JDK URL class) and no host allow-list. When a policy is loaded via the URL/File factory methods (Policy.getInstance(URL) at line 201-203, getInstance(File) at 181-188), the content is normally the application's own configuration; however if an attacker can influence the policy source (e.g., a policy-upload/remote-policy feature), the include mechanism lets them direct the server to fetch arbitrary URLs or read local files. Note CodeQL-style taint from HTML never reaches this code path: getSimpleParseContext (used for InputStream-based policies) explicitly rejects include references (Policy.java:226-231).
missing_evidence: I did not read any Policy getter/validation code beyond line 599 to confirm whether include hrefs are otherwise constrained (e.g., in InternalPolicy).
No application-level code that decides where the policy file comes from was in scope, so attacker influence over policy content is unproven.
No test or config was read demonstrating an include with an external http/file href in this repository.
preconditions: Application loads its policy through Policy.getInstance(URL) or getInstance(File) (Policy.java:181-203), which are the only factories that support <include> (comment at Policy.java:194-195).
An attacker has some ability to influence the policy file content or the baseUrl used for include resolution.

Note: if a policy loaded from URL contains includes, the top-level policy fetch itself already performs network/file IO, so this candidate assumes the policy body is attacker-influenced but its origin is otherwise acceptable.
candidates.title: Policy include href is resolved and opened as an arbitrary URL without scheme/host restriction

counter_evidence: The method only builds a String/URL; by itself it performs no I/O, so exploitability depends entirely on the caller (Policy.getPolicy) and on whether the final URL is opened (Policy.java:340, 347, 358).
New URL guards are applied at several points (lines 69, 99, 132) before returning values.
In the normal AntiSamy flow the policy is trusted configuration, which shrinks the practical attack surface.
candidates.description: URIUtils.resolveAsString first returns the href unchanged if it parses as a URL (lines 66-72), then rebuilds an absolute string from documentBase + href and, on MalformedURLException, treats the input as a local file: it constructs `new File(href)` / `new File(absolute)`, calls getAbsolutePath(), and wraps it in a file:/// URL (lines 116-133). The result is returned even if the file does not exist (line 123 `if (iFile.exists() || (!exists))`). Reachable callers pass attacker-influenced strings into this method (Policy.getPolicy at Policy.java:345 and 356). While resolveAsString does not itself open the stream, returning a `file:///` URL for arbitrary relative paths can convert a later open of the returned value into a local-file read, and normalize() may throw for `..` beyond the root (lines 172-176).
missing_evidence: Only lines 1-200 of URIUtils were read; lines 201-227 (createFileURL and any further checks) were not inspected.
I did not verify whether any production (non-policy) code path exposes resolveAsString to HTML-derived input.
No runtime test demonstrating a file:/// escape was performed.
preconditions: A caller passes attacker-influenced href/documentBase into resolveAsString and opens the returned value (as Policy.getPolicy does with url.openStream(), Policy.java:340/347/358).
The href is not a valid absolute URL and the constructed absolute path does not resolve to a valid URL, so execution reaches the local-file branch (URIUtils.java:116-133).
candidates.title: URIUtils.resolveAsString silently falls back to local file URLs for unresolved hrefs

counter_evidence: The non-importing CssScanner path (chosen when isEmbedStyleSheets() is false, AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:400) does not fetch remote content.
Inline style attribute scanning is always CssScanner (AntiSamyDOMScanner.java:538), so the attribute path cannot trigger imports here.
candidates.description: The importing scanner is selected in two places that both consume the same ExternalCssScanner code: <style> element handling (AntiSamyDOMScanner.processStyleTag, lines 391-401, called from actionValidate at 359-361) and the standalone stylesheet entry point CssScanner.scanStyleSheet, which unconditionally calls parseImportedStylesheets after parsing the sheet (CssScanner.java:150). Because ExternalCssScanner.parseImportedStylesheets performs the network fetch (ExternalCssScanner.java:124-131), any code that routes attacker CSS into a policy with embedStyleSheets enabled reaches the fetch described in candidate 1. This is recorded as a distinct call-site observation to make explicit that the guard is a configuration directive (policy.isEmbedStyleSheets()) rather than an input validation check.
missing_evidence: CssHandler.java (which populates the import list) in CssScanner was not read in the allowed spans; CssScanner lines 1-200 only.
Whether CssValidator delegates to scanStyleSheet with attacker CSS was not verified from source in scope.
preconditions: Attacker-controlled CSS reaches either a <style> element or a direct CssScanner.scanStyleSheet / ExternalCssScanner call.
candidates.title: SSRF via CSS @import is a repeated call-site concern: the importing scan is chosen solely by policy directive
